summary.p: Gothic palimpsest bifolium preserving the undertext of the Gospel of Matthew (25:38-26:3; 26:65-27:1). Verses 26:70-27:1 are also transmitted by the Codex Argenteus. The upper text transmits a portion of Matthew in Latin (28:1-20).

extent.p: The bifolium represents the outer bifolium of a quire, as can be inferred from the missing text. The margins are irregularly trimmed and severely damaged. The written area measures approximately 118 × 153 mm.

condition.p: The bifolium is now disbound and kept in a folder. The margins are damaged, probably due to rodent activity.

layout.p: The Gothic text is arranged in a single column, in scriptio continua. The written area, consisting of 17 lines, is delimited by a single vertical ruling line, executed on the flesh side on the unfolded bifolium, with the aid of pricking marks.

handDesc.handNote: The Gothic text is written in the vertical Gothic script (with <s> of Latin form) by a single scribe, skilled and confident in execution. The proportion between letter height and width is slightly greater than that observed in other manuscripts; the script appears more tense, and the axis of some letters is slightly inclined to the left. Letters of larger module occur, shifted to the left outside the ruling, marking the beginning of a new textual unit. Letters of smaller module, often misaligned, are occasionally attested at the end of the line.
The script of the Latin text is semi-uncial (CLA, III 351); it originally belonged to a codex written in Insular script (CLA, III 350; Zironi 2004, 67, 70).

scriptDesc.p: The Gothic script is vertical Gothic with Latin-form <s>. Letters of larger module mark the beginning of textual units, projecting beyond the ruling. Letters of smaller module, often misaligned, appear at line ends.

decoDesc.decoNote: Dark ink used (not more precisely identifiable). A running title is visible, indicated by monograms consisting of <þ> and <r> for þairh 'according to' on the verso (f. 90v), and <m> and <þ> for maþþaiu 'Matthew' on the recto (f. 91r). They were probably placed on alternating pages. In the left margin, a paragraph mark is attested: a thin oblique stroke slanting to the left, thickened at the ends and bearing at its centre a sign resembling a diplé.

additions.p: The Eusebian sections are not highlighted. In the outer margin of f. 91v, at the beginning of Mt 27:1, however, there is an attestation—isolated among the Gothic witnesses—of a letter that may be interpreted as <k>. The symbol may represent a kephalaion, indicating the beginning of a new textual unit.
A quire number (<ig> = 13 in Gothic script), marking the order of the gatherings, is present in the lower right corner, enclosed within a frame of signs.

The leaves bear a double numbering, written in pencil in the upper outer margin: the first dates from when the codex was still bound (ff. 90 and 91), and the second, more recent, was added after the leaves had been separated, on each page (pp. 1, 2, 3, and 4).
Punctuation: The medial point marks minor pauses (commata), and the colon marks major pauses (cola).
Both nasals are abbreviated at line end, apparently by the same sign (a horizontal stroke thickened at both ends). The usual nomina sacra are present.
The deletion of two letters by means of short strokes placed above them is attested. Not all errors were corrected.
In the external margin of f. 90v there are signs, no longer decipherable, which suggest the presence of glosses; possibly a Greek or runic 's' may be identified.
Phenomena of graphic assimilation are attested, also found in other Gothic manuscripts.

origin.origDate: First third/first half of the sixth century (Gothic undertext)
Second half of the seventh century (Latin overtext)
origin.origPlace: It is highly likely that the original manuscript was copied in an Ostrogothic milieu. It was very probably overwritten at Bobbio (CLA, III 351; Zironi 2004, 67, 70).

provenance.p: The history of the original manuscript is unknown. Codicological features distinguishing it from the Codex Argenteus suggest a different place and/or period of production. The Gothic bifolium was very likely reused at Bobbio to overwrite it with the Gospel text. This codex bears the library ex libris and is mentioned in the inventory of 1461 under number 6 (Zironi 2004, 131).

acquisition.p: Discovered by Angelo Mai in 1815 (Lo Monaco 1996, 689-691), the Gothic text was published together with Castiglioni in 1819 (Ulphilae partium ineditarum in Ambrosianis palimpsestis ab Angelo Maio repertarum specimen, jointly edited by Mai and Carlo Ottavio Castiglioni, Milan, 8-12); the phototypic reproduction of the leaves is found in de Vries 1936.
